title: Show Call
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles describes Show Call, a routine in which student work is displayed under the visualiser or on the board and the teacher chooses whose work to show. He notes that many teachers show only good answers to protect weaker students, and argues that random selection produces better progress. He lists the benefits: accountability, exposure of misconceptions, concrete comparison of answers and a culture in which error is a teaching opportunity. He ties the routine to metacognition, the idea that we learn faster when we realise what we do not know. His classroom sequence is a Silent Solo task followed by Show Call and student annotation of their own work. He uses the driving instructor as a closing analogy for learning quickly through constant correction.
points: Salles argues that picking only strong answers for Show Call protects self-esteem at the cost of learning, while random selection makes all students accountable.
He holds that displaying work exposes common misconceptions and lets students see why one answer is better than another.
He links the routine to metacognition by having students attempt a Silent Solo task first so they discover what they do not know.
He models learning by sampling students to critique note taking and by teaching directly from a standard and an excellent example the next lesson.
His driving instructor analogy claims lessons should work like paid-by-results instruction with constant correction.
quotes: Many teachers are shy of the truth - we often pick volunteers so as not to expose the weaker students. We worry about their self esteem. This becomes really apparent in Show Call, where student work is placed under the visualiser, or projected on the board.
My thinking about learning is that we learn faster when we realise what we don't know, and then do something about it. That's my working definition of meta-cognition, anyway.

By trying some sort of application task in class. In my case, this is a Silent Solo activity - usually writing, sometimes a mind map connecting ideas in a way which demonstrates understanding, or a bullet point essay plan which sequences ideas and facts to build an argument.

While I teach from these, students add notes to their own work. If there is time, they rewrite part of it. If not, fine. To make students accountable, I’ll sample one or two to critique the note taking.
As a rule of thumb, I find it most helpful to think of lesson as a driving instructor. They are paid by results, so students want to learn quickly.

So, did your driving instructor make sure that you corrected your misconceptions? Yes, through constant Show Call. You spent half an hour in the car park, and then 100% of your learning happened in the real world, where the consequence of error was a crash, or injury, or death!
